title: CuTe DSL Decorators Overview
key_concepts: preprocessor parameter for control flow handling
Kernel launch with grid and block configuration
critical_patterns: Use @cute.jit for orchestrating GPU work from the CPU
Common pattern: @cute.kernel for computation, @cute.jit for orchestration
Use preprocessor=True for functions with control flow
constraints: Python functions cannot directly call @kernel functions
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL provides two primary decorators: @cute.jit for host-side JIT-compiled functions and @cute.kernel for GPU kernel functions. The @cute.jit decorator is used for functions that run on the CPU and manage GPU execution, while @cute.kernel is used for defining GPU computations with explicit grid and block configurations. The preprocessor parameter in both decorators controls how loops and conditionals are handled, with the default setting (preprocessor=True) recommended for functions with control flow. JIT caching can be managed with the no_cache parameter, allowing for recompilation when needed. Kernel functions must be launched using the .launch() method, specifying grid and block dimensions. Python functions can call @jit functions directly but cannot call @kernel functions without using .launch(). @jit functions can launch @kernel functions, but @kernel functions cannot call other @kernel functions. A typical pattern involves using @cute.kernel for GPU computation and @cute.jit for orchestrating kernel launches and managing memory. Common pitfalls include forgetting to use .launch() for kernel execution and using @kernel for host-side code. The documentation provides guidance on choosing between the decorators based on the task, with @cute.jit suitable for orchestrating GPU work and @cute.kernel for implementing GPU computations.
